newsitem.title: TURKEY: USDA official defends Turkish/Italian pasta ruling.
newsitem.headline: USDA official defends Turkish/Italian pasta ruling.

text.p: A U.S. decision to take action against Turkey and Italy for alleged dumping of their pasta on the American market was taken after thorough investigation and was in line with international law, a U.S. official said on Tuesday.
Craig Thorn, a senior official at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, was speaking at an international grains conference in southern Turkey.

But Turkish pasta makers said they were still nervous about the future, and industry officials complained about the move to Thorn, who had travelled to southern Turkey to explain Washington's decision to impose anti-dumping duties this year.

The U.S. International trade Commission in July made a final determination that the U.S. pasta industry was materially injured by imports from Italy and Turkey, opening the way for countervailing and anti-dumping duties.
Turkey exported 115,000 tonnes of pasta last year including about 50,000 tonnes to the United States.

Official figures supplied at the conference by the foreign trade undersecretariat showed Turkey imported 1.253 million tonnes of wheat in calendar 1995, of which 1.2 million tonnes was milling wheat. The balance was pasta-making durum wheat.

Turkey on Saturday raised taxes on wheat and corn imports to 15 percent from three percent in an effort to encourage local millers and pasta producers to use local crops after an expected rise in both the wheat and corn harvests.
Turkish pasta producers, whose exports are second only to those of Italy, have already said they would continue wheat imports regardless of the increase in the import tax, which will raise costs.
